title: Komi is not calibrated from results
why: You asked whether komi is already centred on the point where Black and White are even. It isn't. bulk-loop.sh sets the centre by hand (coefficient 28.0, about 7 points) and samples komi up to 78% either side of it. generation.rs mentions a fit_komi_power_law that would refit it from games, but that function does not exist. Measured over this run, Black won about 10% of small-board games and 30% of big-board games, and even the lowest komi in the range left Black behind.
ask: Should the loop refit the komi centre per board from recent games, aiming at a 50% win rate? I'd do it after random-stop, since the stalled games are part of why White wins, and record the fit in the run's events.

title: Branch collapse-recipe is ready to merge
why: Commits on top of main: value-label thinning (--value-stride, --value-labels-per-game), weight decay, packed ownership and uint8 ridge (window 107 to 57 KiB a sample), training-only history planes, and the tracker and findings updates. All default off or lossless except the ridge, which matched fp16 on held-out loss. correctness/check.sh passes on the rebuilt binaries.
ask: Merge into main? Pushing stays your call.

title: Rebuild and check the Rust side after the Fedora upgrade

result: Rebuilt in release mode on 2026-11-04; correctness/check.sh passed (Rust, 154 training and 33 dashboard tests).

title: Arena the value recipe, then adopt it
why: The value head memorized its window: train MAE 0.03, held-out 0.65. On update 23's 450k window, 16 labels per game cut held-out value MSE from 0.99 to 0.58 and lifted the winner from 71% to 79%. Policy KL fell as the value weight dropped and was flat at the no-value bound for weights of 1/8 and below. Stride-8 thinning plus weight decay already beat update 23 116-84. All held-out numbers are one seed.
test: Arena the 16-labels, weight-1/16 nets on update 23's window against update 23 and its twin on the 38 board, about 200 games. Two seeds. Then wire --value-labels-per-game 16 --value-weight 0.0625 and a 450k window into bulk-loop.sh.
progress: Training two seeds on update 23's 150k window (8 epochs, as update 23 was), then 200 games against update 23 and its twin on the 38 board.

title: Fix the rating pipeline
why: evaluation/ratings.py could not parse the loop's anchor records (its regex stops one level of nesting short of candidate_search.reuse), and the dashboard's strength curve anchors on sl-w64b16, which this run never plays. A fresh run would have no visible strength curve.
test: Parse anchor.jsonl from artifacts/vgo-bulk, anchor the curve on the run's own update 0, and show updates 3 to 29 on the dashboard with error bars.
result: evaluation/ratings.py parses nested records (27 matches, 162 games of this run now read). The dashboard anchors on the run's earliest update when the supervised baseline never played, so the strength curve shows. The rating prior drops from 2 virtual games to 0.1: at about 6 games a pairing the old prior halved the curve (update 8 +323 against +627). Rating rounds in bulk-loop.sh now play the 38 board at its 312-ply cap, and the reserved reference is the model 6 updates back instead of a fixed update 0, which leaves the pool once the run passes update 6. Cost: 18 big-board games every 3 updates, about 15-30 minutes of shared GPU, until random-stop shortens games.

title: Report value MSE or log loss, not MAE
why: MAE ranked an overconfident value head best: stride-8 thinning read 0.56 MAE but 0.70 MSE against 0.59 MSE for 16 labels per game. The learner's selection score and logs use MAE.
test: Add value MSE and cross-entropy to evaluate(), and use one of them in the selection score.

title: End one-sided pass streaks at random, as a bootstrap
why: 72% of big-board games with a long pass streak ran to the 312-ply cap, so labels read who leads at ply 312. Once a side has passed 4 times running, ending the game with probability 0.25 on each further pass would have ended 74% of big-board games early, about 61 plies sooner, and changed the eventual winner in 13% of those. A stopgap until the value head supports hard resignation: no model input or search change, so it comes out cleanly.
test: Implement in self-play and arena only, seeded for reproducible digests. Check the share of capped games and plies per game in a short run.
progress: Design agreed: self-play and arena only, no model input or search change, seeded.

title: Check the repeated points are board-unchanged self-captures
why: In recorded games the side behind alternated between the same two coordinates for about 150 plies. Your read: the move is a one-stone self-capture, so the board after it equals the board before, the net sees the same input, and it picks the same point again. Self-captures rose from 3% to 8-10% of plies over the run, which fits.
test: Replay the recorded positions: confirm the board is identical before and after each repeated move. If so, a move that leaves the board unchanged is a pass in disguise, which is a rule question for 5b4efdee.

title: Stop the naive generator once its window is full
why: The first update of a fresh run took 64 minutes against about 9, because the naive generator kept all 32 threads while training prepared batches, and it wrote 38 GB of games nobody trains on. Stopping it by hand brought the card straight back.
test: Touch the stop file when the first training starts, and confirm a fresh run's first update finishes in about 10 minutes.
progress: Not started. Matters for the fresh run's first update.

test: After value-recipe, random-stop, ratings-fix and naive-stop: start from the naive generator with the new recipe, and watch the rating curve for the rise-then-fall shape.

title: Let komi follow the result per board
why: Black's self-play win rate fell to about 10% on small boards and 30% on big ones, and the fitted fair komi was often below the sampler's floor. Partly a game-end effect, so decide after random-stop.

revisit: After random-stop, or sooner if you answer review-komi.

title: Train the faster net shapes
why: Fewer blocks, no attention and one norm take the card's ceiling at 128 from 21k positions/s to as much as 62k, but the generator stops gaining near 40k here. Trained nets read 30k for `blocks8` (no policy penalty in a loss screen), 35k for `c_d222_short_n1` (+0.013 KL) and 37k for `m_d111_c22` (+0.022 KL), against a seed spread of 0.003. Early in a run generation speed matters more than play, and any net's games train any shape, so a fast shape could generate first and the run could retrain to a stronger one later. Strength is unmeasured, and these rates need 15 to 20 vCPU per card: on 8 threads of 4 cores `blocks8` lost its whole gain within three minutes.
test: Arena `blocks8`, `c_d222_short_n1` and `m_d111_c22` against the current net at equal time on both boards, about 500 games each. Check a trained one over whole games on 8 vCPU. Checkpoints are in `artifacts/shape-screen/runs/`, and the dashboard's Net shapes tab shows the screen.
revisit: When choosing the net for the later, stronger phase of a run. m_d111_c22 already generates early.

title: Settle one norm per block
why: About 15% more positions/s at the card's ceiling, with mixed, inconclusive arenas: 86-106 over four small matches. The GPU is the limit on throughput at 128.
test: Train it with the faster net shapes, on the same window as their control.
revisit: With faster-net: train it on the same window as their control.

title: Cut the CPU work inside inference lanes
why: At 192 the lighter net reads 16.4k positions/s in the generator against a 23k card ceiling, with the CPU 60% idle. Each lane spends 28% of its time packing inputs and materializing outputs, about 1.1 ms a batch, and the card waits. A third lane makes it worse. Applying the board rotation twice per batch also wastes training CPU: the second call only needs the ownership map.
test: Time `input_packing` and `output_materialization` in broker telemetry before and after, then confirm in the generator.
revisit: Before renting: the home box is GPU-bound, but rented boxes have fewer CPUs per GPU.

title: Measure self-play on rented hardware
why: Here 8 vCPU hold 18.1k positions/s at 128 over whole games, at 95% GPU. A faster card needs more, about 5 vCPU per 10k positions/s by extrapolation, and rented hardware has different wake-up costs, so it needs checking on the real box.
test: Run 64 actors at 128 for 7 minutes pinned to half the cores, so games finish, and record positions/s, GPU use and busy cores.
revisit: Before renting hardware for a long run.

title: Spend search where it can change the result
why: Soft resignation is one narrow case of a general budget question: where does more search change the outcome, and where is it wasted? Framed that way, a yes-or-no concession becomes a search budget that follows how result-affecting the next moves are. There is no direct metric for this yet.
test: Record per-ply root value, KL(search policy || prior) and the value gap between the top two moves in a fresh run. See which of them predicts the result changing, then try a budget that follows it. info-metric is the first step. The dashboard's Reports tab has the ideas report.

title: Measure information per search directly
why: Nothing measures how much a search teaches. KL(search policy || prior) and value change per search would give a real signal-per-compute number.
test: Log both per position in a short run, and check they separate full searches from cheap ones.

title: Sweep the number of history steps
why: 3 plies of history cut held-out policy KL from 1.721 to 1.706 (top-1 0.122 to 0.127) with value unchanged, one seed, at 11 GB more training memory. Not needed yet. --history-plies exists in training; the Rust raster does not render the planes.
test: Train 1, 2, 3 and 4 plies on one window and compare held-out policy KL. If 1 ply carries most of it, render it in Rust and arena it.
revisit: After the fresh run is healthy.

title: Confirm 128 input as the efficient default
why: 128 searches 2-3.6x faster and scored 30-18 at equal time on the big board. One card plays 18.6k positions/s at 128, 7.4k at 192 and 4.1k at 256, so at 61 Elo a doubling 192 has to beat 128 by about 80 Elo at equal simulations and 256 by about 130.
test: Bootstrap at 128. Train a 192 net from scratch on the same window, then play them at equal time with --opponent-resolution on both boards. Move up once it wins.
